title: Indra Stays 101 Years
hook: a god and a demon go to learn the self; the demon leaves happy with the wrong answer, and Indra keeps coming back
carry: moksha: freedom from the round of birth and death
tomorrow: Arjuna asks to see Krishna as he really is. why does he need new eyes?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramanuja's promise: every Vedanta school writes on the same shared books.

Near the end of the Chandogya Upanishad, Prajapati, the creator, announces: there is a self free from old age, death, grief, hunger and thirst. Whoever finds it gains everything. The gods send Indra. The asuras send their king, Virochana. They live as students for thirty-two years. Then Prajapati tells them: look at yourselves in a pan of water, dressed in your best. That's the self. Virochana goes home delighted. The body is the self! And that's what he teaches. Indra gets halfway home and stops. Wait. If the body grows old and dies, that can't be it.
screen: `A SELF BEYOND DEATH AND GRIEF.` → `VIROCHANA: IT'S THE BODY!` → `INDRA: WAIT.`

segments.voice: So Indra goes back. Thirty-two more years. Prajapati says: the self is the one who roams in dreams. Indra thinks it over: but in dreams you can still suffer. Back again, thirty-two more years. The self is the one in deep sleep. But then you know nothing at all. Back once more, five more years, a hundred and one in all. And Prajapati finally says: this body is mortal, held by death, but it's the home of the self that doesn't die. That's the teaching: atman, the self, isn't the body, and knowing it frees you. Hindus call that freedom moksha, release from samsara, the round of birth, death and rebirth. The Chandogya ends with the one who reaches Brahman: he does not return, he does not return. And the Brahma Sutra, which opened with now, the wish to know, closes the same way: no return, said twice. The schools fill in what freedom is. For Shankara, it's knowing what was always so: the self was never anything but Brahman. For Ramanuja and Madhva, the freed self stays itself and lives with the Lord, whom they know as Vishnu, in a joy that doesn't end. So when an elder says she prays not to come back, she isn't asking for less life. She's asking for freedom. Like Indra, she just wants the real answer.
screen: `DREAM? DEEP SLEEP? KEEP GOING.` · `THE SELF ISN'T THE BODY.` · `NO RETURN, SAID TWICE.` · `SHE'S ASKING FOR FREEDOM.`

segments.voice: Sit and notice your body, the weight, the warmth. That's known. Then notice your thoughts passing, like a dream. That's known too. Then ask gently, like Indra: who is knowing all this? Don't answer. Rest in the knowing for a few breaths. If you pray, you can rest in the presence of the One you pray to.
Vedanta. From the first word, now, the wish to know, to the last, no return, said twice: freedom. Today's word, and the last of our visit with it.
Your line: moksha, freedom from the round of birth and death. Like Indra, don't stop at the first answer. Rest well.

screen: `DAY 1196 COUNTS.` → `MOKSHA: FREEDOM FROM THE ROUND OF BIRTH AND DEATH.` → `TOMORROW: WHY DOES ARJUNA NEED NEW EYES?`

howItsDone: Hindus speak of moksha, release from samsara, as life's highest aim, and many elders pray for it; traditional students read the Brahma Sutra from its first line to its last, 'no return', said twice, usually through their own lineage's commentary.

fork.setup: Prajapati says the self is the one who dreams. Indra notices dreamers still suffer. what does he do?
options: accept it and go home, like Virochana
decide there is no self at all
fork.reveal: he goes back, 101 years in all, until he hears of the deathless self. that's the seeker's way in Vedanta.

chat.meaning: Indra went back to Prajapati for 101 years to find the deathless self; the Chandogya and the Brahma Sutra end with 'no return', freedom from samsara, which Hindus call moksha.

tie.story: Indra kept going back to Prajapati, 101 years in all, until he learned the self that doesn't die.

Indra.meaning: king of the gods, who kept going back to learn the self

Virochana.meaning: king of the asuras, who took the body for the self

Prajapati.meaning: the creator, teacher of Indra and Virochana

moksha.meaning: release from the round of birth and death

samsara.meaning: the round of birth, death and rebirth

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 8.7-8.12 (Prajapati's teaching; Indra and Virochana; the reflection, the dreamer, deep sleep; 101 years; the mortal body as the home of the deathless self)

notes: Brahma Sutra 4.4.22 anavrittih shabdat anavrittih shabdat: confirm the repetition and the paraphrase 'on the word of scripture'.
'Saying the closing words twice signals the end' is a general claim about Sanskrit texts (repetition marking the close of a chapter or work); confirm or soften to 'tradition reads the repetition as'.
Chandogya 8.15.1 ends na ca punar avartate, na ca punar avartate; confirm the echo.

The schools' accounts of liberation are compressed: Shankara (realizing identity, no going anywhere) versus Ramanuja and Madhva (the freed self in Vishnu's presence, in bliss). Madhva's gradations among the freed are left out. Confirm.
